medical.title: Spatial mapping of growth plate tissue may help explain how bones grow
medical.summary: Researchers at the Department of Women's and Children's Health have used a novel technique to map which genes are active in different regions of the skeleton's growth plates. The findings offer new clues about how the body controls bone elongation—and why certain genetic mutations lead to skeletal disorders. The study is published in the journal Bone Research.

medical.title: Systemic gap in drug subsidies leaves low-income pregnant women with fewer treatment options
medical.summary: Pregnant women in Australia are facing an unfair two-tiered system for managing morning sickness, with financial status affecting who can access the full range of modern anti-nausea medications available rather than simply clinical need.

medical.title: Once‑weekly HIV pill as effective as daily dose, research shows
medical.summary: Around 78% of people living with HIV take a daily pill to manage their infection. These drugs work by preventing HIV from multiplying.

medical.title: Common neuroscience sensors sometimes get their signals crossed
medical.summary: Cells in the brain communicate in different ways. The classical mode involves tight connections between individual cells that signal only to each other. But over the last decade, new tools have allowed scientists to focus increasingly on other, more diffuse systems in which brain chemicals called neuromodulators communicate with many different cells over longer time frames.

medical.title: The value of a refusal: Research targets engagement gaps in opioid overdose care
medical.summary: The most important people in a clinical trial may be the ones who never join it. Every "no" in a clinical trial is usually treated as the end of a conversation, but a new MUSC study suggests it might be the beginning of an important one. The study is published in the Journal of Substance Use and Addiction Treatment.

medical.title: New model maps where HIV is concentrated and the disease is more advanced
medical.summary: A new biostatistical modeling approach has the potential to support health decisions by pinpointing where HIV is concentrated and where people living with HIV are showing signs of severe immune suppression or delayed treatment. Published in iScience, the study shows the potential of using existing health data to identify both where HIV burden is concentrated and where different forms of prevention, treatment and support may be needed.

medical.title: Childhood physical illnesses linked to increased risk of mental health disorders in autistic young adults
medical.summary: Mental health conditions are more common among autistic individuals than in the general population, but knowledge about how physical and mental health interact over time has been limited. In the new study, researchers analyzed data from nearly 2 million individuals born in Sweden between 1985 and 2004, including more than 58,000 people diagnosed with autism.

medical.title: Mindfulness-based therapy for opioid misuse can offer massive return on investment
medical.summary: A new economic evaluation from the University of California San Diego School of Medicine has revealed that Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE)—an innovative, evidence-based, neuroscience-informed therapy for opioid misuse and chronic pain—provides $12 in cost savings for every dollar spent, between two and six times as cost-effective as other addiction treatments such as residential or intensive outpatient treatment. Over the course of a patient's life, the analysis found that these savings totaled more than $324,000 per patient.

medical.title: Early mental health support before birth may help prevent postpartum depression
medical.summary: Each morning during rounds as a resident at University of Rochester Medicine, Marika Toscano noticed the same troubling pattern.

medical.title: RNA technology improves insulin-producing cell transplantation outcomes
medical.summary: Researchers from the Rolf Luft Research Center for Diabetes and Endocrinology at Karolinska Institutet have developed a targeted RNA technology to prepare pancreatic islet cells for transplantation. The technology briefly boosts a gene that drives blood vessel growth, prompting grafts to re-establish their blood supply sooner and shortening the vulnerable, low-oxygen window that normally follows transplantation. In studies using both mouse and human islets, treated cells engrafted more effectively and required fewer donor islets to restore normal blood sugar control.

medical.title: Most people with eating disorders don't receive specialist NHS referral
medical.summary: A study of GP records for more than 35,000 adults in England and Northern Ireland has found that most people diagnosed with an eating disorder are never referred to specialist NHS treatment and that body weight plays a large part in who is seen and who is not. Using anonymized primary care data from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD Aurum), covering records from 2010 to 2023, researchers identified 35,404 adults ages 18–80 with at least one eating disorder diagnosis, of whom 26,822, or 75.8%, had no record of referral to specialist services.

medical.title: Your AI calorie-tracking app may be off by 345 calories
medical.summary: Popular AI-powered food apps may make calorie counting easier, but they may also leave out a surprisingly large part of the meal. Four apps underestimated calories and fat by about one-third when tested against carefully prepared meals. High-fat ketogenic dishes appeared to cause the most trouble, while carbohydrates were measured more consistently.

medical.title: CRISPR makes prostate cancer vulnerable to immunotherapy
medical.summary: Scientists used CRISPR to make prostate cancer cells easier for the immune system to detect and destroy. The experimental treatment dramatically improved the effects of immunotherapy in mice and may offer hope for other hard-to-treat tumors.

medical.title: Why losing the wrong fat can trigger diabetes
medical.summary: Scientists discovered that damaged fat cells can become inflamed, lose their ability to store lipids, and eventually vanish, disrupting the body’s metabolism. The findings show that diabetes can result not only from excess fat, but also from losing the healthy fat tissue the body needs.

medical.title: Watching too much TV in midlife may shrink the brain
medical.summary: Watching television very often in midlife may be linked to troubling brain changes decades later. In a study of about 1,700 adults, frequent TV viewers later showed smaller brain regions involved in memory, decision-making, and visual processing, along with more signs of damage in the brain’s white matter. Surprisingly, sitting itself did not appear to be the main issue, since people who spent long hours seated at mentally engaging jobs often showed healthier brain patterns.

medical.title: Scientists found mystery bacteria inside one of the ocean’s most elusive whales
medical.summary: Scientists studying decades of pygmy sperm whale strandings have uncovered three previously unknown types of Helicobacter bacteria hiding in the animals’ stomachs. All four infected whales showed serious digestive damage, including inflammation, ulcers, scarring, and parasite infestations, although the bacteria were not confirmed as the cause of death.

medical.title: New molecular map reveals how the flu virus hijacks human cells
medical.summary: Scientists uncovered how influenza A commandeers human cells, including a surprising strategy that dissolves tiny structures in the nucleus and releases proteins the virus may use to reproduce. The detailed molecular map could reveal new drug targets and help researchers study dangerous flu strains such as H5N1.

science.title: Scattered Roman bones point to potential fourth-century purge at Brading Villa
science.summary: Disarticulated bones found scattered across a luxurious Roman villa on England's Isle of Wight may be evidence of a massacre carried out during a brutal political purge in the fourth century, a new study in Britannia suggests.

science.title: SpaceX aims to use rockets to quickly transport cargo across the Earth and into orbit
science.summary: You might think of rockets as powerful vehicles that blast astronaut crews and robotic missions into space. But what if they could be used to send cargo from one side of Earth to the other in a fraction of the time it would take a plane? The company SpaceX recently announced a project that aims to use its rockets to do just that.

science.title: Cell-inspired synthetic fibers reveal a reversible route to self-protecting smart materials
science.summary: Researchers at the University of Bayreuth, together with colleagues from Freie Universität Berlin and the Leibniz Institute of Polymer Research Dresden, have developed a synthetic fiber system inspired by the cellular cytoskeleton that protects itself through controlled bundling. The findings open up new avenues for smart, switchable materials whose properties can be deliberately altered in response to a specific stimulus. The research is published in the journal Advanced Materials.

science.title: Restoring the silenced Friedreich's ataxia gene through unconventional means
science.summary: Cells can switch off genes by tightly packaging DNA around proteins called histones. However, scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital have discovered that under certain conditions, this packaging acts more like molasses than a solid, allowing a specially designed chemical adapter to shuttle gene-activating proteins through the packaging to the silenced gene inside. In addition, the researchers showed that this process reactivates the gene frataxin, which is abnormally silenced in the neurodegenerative disease Friedreich's ataxia. The study, published today in Nature Cell Biology, challenges a longstanding assumption that histone chemical modifications operate in a simple "on" or "off" binary manner.

science.title: Is hemp a thirsty crop? New research measures just how much water cannabis farming can use
science.summary: In South Africa, it's been legal for several years for people to grow hemp (a type of Cannabis sativa with very low levels of the psychoactive compound THC) for personal use following changes to the law. There's also been a growing interest in its medicinal and industrial potential for clothing, insulation and paper production. Many see it as a "green gold" opportunity for small-scale farmers.

science.title: New molecule class creates hardy, drought tolerant plants
science.summary: As climate change causes water scarcity and temperatures to rise, crops around the world are feeling the heat. How can we prevent severe crop losses in these relentlessly sweltering conditions? An international research team led by Tohoku University has identified a new class of small molecules that enhances plant drought tolerance without any major negative impact on plant growth.

science.title: Social media can shape your travel plans, according to study
science.summary: New University of Georgia research suggests that social media could influence people's travel plans. The paper is published in the journal Current Issues in Tourism.

science.title: Gene-edited beagles may offer a future option for people with dog allergies
science.summary: Matt Walker couldn't pet a dog without sneezing—until he and other scientists used a gene editing technique to produce a hypoallergenic beagle named Bailey.

science.title: NASA’s Perseverance Rover Watches Earth Vanish Behind Martian Moon
science.summary: Earth and the Martian moon Phobos dance together in a series of images recently acquired by NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover. Earth appears as a point of light in the Martian sky, disappearing behind the crescent of Phobos, the larger of Mars’ two moons. This is the first time humanity has captured from the surface of […]

science.title: Human activity more than doubles Arctic fire occurrence, satellite analysis suggests
science.summary: Fires in the Arctic are not solely a regional issue, as shown by the hazy skies in Switzerland last summer despite otherwise sunny weather. Smoke from major fires in northern Canada crossed the Atlantic and reached Europe. Until now, large-scale studies of Arctic tundra fires have focused primarily on rising temperatures and drought as the main drivers. The role of human activity has received much less attention, even as industrial development, settlements, roads and other infrastructure expand rapidly in parts of the Arctic, particularly in connection with extractive industries such as oil and gas production and mining.

environment.title: Bornean ferret badger only lives in Borneo. Could it be a conservation symbol?
environment.summary: The Bornean ferret badger is a small carnivore with the slinky body of a ferret and a face mask like a badger. A new study confirms that it lives only in the mountains of Sabah, a Malaysian state on the island of Borneo. Ferret badgers are nocturnal carnivores, widespread across Southeast Asia, but the Bornean […]

environment.title: Mozambique completes first white rhino breeding population in decades
environment.summary: On June 6, nine female white rhinos arrived in Mozambique’s Zinave National Park following a two-day translocation. Their arrival marks the culmination of nearly 10 years of rhino reintroduction efforts in the park, aimed at rebuilding a viable breeding population of the mammals in Zinave after decades of local extinction. The white rhinos (Ceratotherium simum) […]

environment.title: ‘Flamingo Revolution’ aims to stop Kushner-backed resort on protected Albanian delta
environment.summary: VJOSA-NARTA, Albania — In late April, heavy machinery began moving into the Pishë Poro-Narta protected landscape on Albania’s Adriatic coast without permits or public notice. Bulldozers and excavators felled coastal pine trees, flattened sand dunes, and cut new roads through previously untouched habitat. Then, barbed wire fences went up along the shoreline. The incursion was […]

environment.title: The secret underground system keeping the Grand Canyon alive
environment.summary: Scientists are venturing into the Grand Canyon’s hidden cave networks to solve a mystery: how snowmelt travels underground to supply the park’s vital springs. Their discoveries could help protect the canyon’s water from drought, contamination, and other growing threats.

environment.title: DNA solves 250-year-old mystery of the Seychelles’ lost crocodiles
environment.summary: Scientists have solved the mystery of the Seychelles’ vanished crocodiles using DNA from historic museum specimens. The reptiles were not a unique species after all, but an isolated population of saltwater crocodiles that likely drifted thousands of kilometers across the Indian Ocean.

environment.title: Scottish wrens may be evolving into new species through island gigantism
environment.summary: Tiny birds on remote Scottish islands are undergoing a dramatic evolutionary transformation. Scientists studying four isolated populations of British Wrens discovered that some island birds have grown astonishingly large — with the biggest St Kilda Wrens weighing more than twice as much as the smallest mainland birds. The research suggests these wrens are evolving independently, developing unique songs, appearances, and genetics that may eventually turn them into entirely new species.

environment.title: A New York cemetery was hiding 5.5 million bees underground
environment.summary: A casual walk through an Ithaca cemetery led to the discovery of a gigantic hidden bee population — roughly 5.5 million ground-nesting bees packed beneath the soil. Scientists believe it may be one of the largest bee aggregations ever documented and say the insects are crucial pollinators for apple orchards and other crops. The bees have likely lived there for more than 100 years, thriving in the cemetery’s undisturbed sandy soil.

environment.title: Earth’s orbital wobble triggered rapid climate chaos during the dinosaur age
environment.summary: New research suggests Earth’s climate can swing wildly on surprisingly short timescales — even during hot, ice-free greenhouse periods. By studying ancient sediments from the Late Cretaceous, scientists uncovered repeating climate shifts tied to tiny changes in Earth’s orbital wobble. These cycles may have repeatedly pushed the planet between humid and arid states every few thousand years.

mix_items.title: Scattered Roman bones point to potential fourth-century purge at Brading Villa
mix_items.summary: Disarticulated bones found scattered across a luxurious Roman villa on England's Isle of Wight may be evidence of a massacre carried out during a brutal political purge in the fourth century, a new study in Britannia suggests.

mix_items.title: Spatial mapping of growth plate tissue may help explain how bones grow
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Department of Women's and Children's Health have used a novel technique to map which genes are active in different regions of the skeleton's growth plates. The findings offer new clues about how the body controls bone elongation—and why certain genetic mutations lead to skeletal disorders. The study is published in the journal Bone Research.

mix_items.summary: Pregnant women in Australia are facing an unfair two-tiered system for managing morning sickness, with financial status affecting who can access the full range of modern anti-nausea medications available rather than simply clinical need.

mix_items.title: SpaceX aims to use rockets to quickly transport cargo across the Earth and into orbit
mix_items.summary: You might think of rockets as powerful vehicles that blast astronaut crews and robotic missions into space. But what if they could be used to send cargo from one side of Earth to the other in a fraction of the time it would take a plane? The company SpaceX recently announced a project that aims to use its rockets to do just that.

mix_items.title: Inocenți, locul în care curajul crește pas cu pas
mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea Alinei și cum sprijinul oferit de Fundația Inocenți a ajutat-o să își dezvolte încrederea în sine, abilitățile școlare și curajul de a reuși. The post Inocenți, locul în care curajul crește pas cu pas appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Once‑weekly HIV pill as effective as daily dose, research shows
mix_items.summary: Around 78% of people living with HIV take a daily pill to manage their infection. These drugs work by preventing HIV from multiplying.

mix_items.title: Common neuroscience sensors sometimes get their signals crossed
mix_items.summary: Cells in the brain communicate in different ways. The classical mode involves tight connections between individual cells that signal only to each other. But over the last decade, new tools have allowed scientists to focus increasingly on other, more diffuse systems in which brain chemicals called neuromodulators communicate with many different cells over longer time frames.

mix_items.title: Cell-inspired synthetic fibers reveal a reversible route to self-protecting smart materials
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Bayreuth, together with colleagues from Freie Universität Berlin and the Leibniz Institute of Polymer Research Dresden, have developed a synthetic fiber system inspired by the cellular cytoskeleton that protects itself through controlled bundling. The findings open up new avenues for smart, switchable materials whose properties can be deliberately altered in response to a specific stimulus. The research is published in the journal Advanced Materials.

mix_items.title: Restoring the silenced Friedreich's ataxia gene through unconventional means
mix_items.summary: Cells can switch off genes by tightly packaging DNA around proteins called histones. However, scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital have discovered that under certain conditions, this packaging acts more like molasses than a solid, allowing a specially designed chemical adapter to shuttle gene-activating proteins through the packaging to the silenced gene inside. In addition, the researchers showed that this process reactivates the gene frataxin, which is abnormally silenced in the neurodegenerative disease Friedreich's ataxia. The study, published today in Nature Cell Biology, challenges a longstanding assumption that histone chemical modifications operate in a simple "on" or "off" binary manner.

mix_items.title: The value of a refusal: Research targets engagement gaps in opioid overdose care
mix_items.summary: The most important people in a clinical trial may be the ones who never join it. Every "no" in a clinical trial is usually treated as the end of a conversation, but a new MUSC study suggests it might be the beginning of an important one. The study is published in the Journal of Substance Use and Addiction Treatment.

mix_items.title: Is hemp a thirsty crop? New research measures just how much water cannabis farming can use
mix_items.summary: In South Africa, it's been legal for several years for people to grow hemp (a type of Cannabis sativa with very low levels of the psychoactive compound THC) for personal use following changes to the law. There's also been a growing interest in its medicinal and industrial potential for clothing, insulation and paper production. Many see it as a "green gold" opportunity for small-scale farmers.

mix_items.title: New model maps where HIV is concentrated and the disease is more advanced
mix_items.summary: A new biostatistical modeling approach has the potential to support health decisions by pinpointing where HIV is concentrated and where people living with HIV are showing signs of severe immune suppression or delayed treatment. Published in iScience, the study shows the potential of using existing health data to identify both where HIV burden is concentrated and where different forms of prevention, treatment and support may be needed.

mix_items.title: Childhood physical illnesses linked to increased risk of mental health disorders in autistic young adults
mix_items.summary: Mental health conditions are more common among autistic individuals than in the general population, but knowledge about how physical and mental health interact over time has been limited. In the new study, researchers analyzed data from nearly 2 million individuals born in Sweden between 1985 and 2004, including more than 58,000 people diagnosed with autism.

mix_items.title: Mindfulness-based therapy for opioid misuse can offer massive return on investment
mix_items.summary: A new economic evaluation from the University of California San Diego School of Medicine has revealed that Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE)—an innovative, evidence-based, neuroscience-informed therapy for opioid misuse and chronic pain—provides $12 in cost savings for every dollar spent, between two and six times as cost-effective as other addiction treatments such as residential or intensive outpatient treatment. Over the course of a patient's life, the analysis found that these savings totaled more than $324,000 per patient.

mix_items.title: New molecule class creates hardy, drought tolerant plants
mix_items.summary: As climate change causes water scarcity and temperatures to rise, crops around the world are feeling the heat. How can we prevent severe crop losses in these relentlessly sweltering conditions? An international research team led by Tohoku University has identified a new class of small molecules that enhances plant drought tolerance without any major negative impact on plant growth.

mix_items.title: Early mental health support before birth may help prevent postpartum depression
mix_items.summary: Each morning during rounds as a resident at University of Rochester Medicine, Marika Toscano noticed the same troubling pattern.

mix_items.title: RNA technology improves insulin-producing cell transplantation outcomes
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the Rolf Luft Research Center for Diabetes and Endocrinology at Karolinska Institutet have developed a targeted RNA technology to prepare pancreatic islet cells for transplantation. The technology briefly boosts a gene that drives blood vessel growth, prompting grafts to re-establish their blood supply sooner and shortening the vulnerable, low-oxygen window that normally follows transplantation. In studies using both mouse and human islets, treated cells engrafted more effectively and required fewer donor islets to restore normal blood sugar control.

mix_items.title: Social media can shape your travel plans, according to study
mix_items.summary: New University of Georgia research suggests that social media could influence people's travel plans. The paper is published in the journal Current Issues in Tourism.

mix_items.title: Gene-edited beagles may offer a future option for people with dog allergies
mix_items.summary: Matt Walker couldn't pet a dog without sneezing—until he and other scientists used a gene editing technique to produce a hypoallergenic beagle named Bailey.

mix_items.title: NASA’s Perseverance Rover Watches Earth Vanish Behind Martian Moon
mix_items.summary: Earth and the Martian moon Phobos dance together in a series of images recently acquired by NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover. Earth appears as a point of light in the Martian sky, disappearing behind the crescent of Phobos, the larger of Mars’ two moons. This is the first time humanity has captured from the surface of […]

mix_items.title: Human activity more than doubles Arctic fire occurrence, satellite analysis suggests
mix_items.summary: Fires in the Arctic are not solely a regional issue, as shown by the hazy skies in Switzerland last summer despite otherwise sunny weather. Smoke from major fires in northern Canada crossed the Atlantic and reached Europe. Until now, large-scale studies of Arctic tundra fires have focused primarily on rising temperatures and drought as the main drivers. The role of human activity has received much less attention, even as industrial development, settlements, roads and other infrastructure expand rapidly in parts of the Arctic, particularly in connection with extractive industries such as oil and gas production and mining.

mix_items.title: Most people with eating disorders don't receive specialist NHS referral
mix_items.summary: A study of GP records for more than 35,000 adults in England and Northern Ireland has found that most people diagnosed with an eating disorder are never referred to specialist NHS treatment and that body weight plays a large part in who is seen and who is not. Using anonymized primary care data from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD Aurum), covering records from 2010 to 2023, researchers identified 35,404 adults ages 18–80 with at least one eating disorder diagnosis, of whom 26,822, or 75.8%, had no record of referral to specialist services.

mix_items.title: Bornean ferret badger only lives in Borneo. Could it be a conservation symbol?
mix_items.summary: The Bornean ferret badger is a small carnivore with the slinky body of a ferret and a face mask like a badger. A new study confirms that it lives only in the mountains of Sabah, a Malaysian state on the island of Borneo. Ferret badgers are nocturnal carnivores, widespread across Southeast Asia, but the Bornean […]

mix_items.title: Mozambique completes first white rhino breeding population in decades
mix_items.summary: On June 6, nine female white rhinos arrived in Mozambique’s Zinave National Park following a two-day translocation. Their arrival marks the culmination of nearly 10 years of rhino reintroduction efforts in the park, aimed at rebuilding a viable breeding population of the mammals in Zinave after decades of local extinction. The white rhinos (Ceratotherium simum) […]

mix_items.title: ‘Flamingo Revolution’ aims to stop Kushner-backed resort on protected Albanian delta
mix_items.summary: VJOSA-NARTA, Albania — In late April, heavy machinery began moving into the Pishë Poro-Narta protected landscape on Albania’s Adriatic coast without permits or public notice. Bulldozers and excavators felled coastal pine trees, flattened sand dunes, and cut new roads through previously untouched habitat. Then, barbed wire fences went up along the shoreline. The incursion was […]

mix_items.title: Your AI calorie-tracking app may be off by 345 calories
mix_items.summary: Popular AI-powered food apps may make calorie counting easier, but they may also leave out a surprisingly large part of the meal. Four apps underestimated calories and fat by about one-third when tested against carefully prepared meals. High-fat ketogenic dishes appeared to cause the most trouble, while carbohydrates were measured more consistently.

mix_items.title: CRISPR makes prostate cancer vulnerable to immunotherapy
mix_items.summary: Scientists used CRISPR to make prostate cancer cells easier for the immune system to detect and destroy. The experimental treatment dramatically improved the effects of immunotherapy in mice and may offer hope for other hard-to-treat tumors.

mix_items.title: Why losing the wrong fat can trigger diabetes
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered that damaged fat cells can become inflamed, lose their ability to store lipids, and eventually vanish, disrupting the body’s metabolism. The findings show that diabetes can result not only from excess fat, but also from losing the healthy fat tissue the body needs.

mix_items.title: Watching too much TV in midlife may shrink the brain
mix_items.summary: Watching television very often in midlife may be linked to troubling brain changes decades later. In a study of about 1,700 adults, frequent TV viewers later showed smaller brain regions involved in memory, decision-making, and visual processing, along with more signs of damage in the brain’s white matter. Surprisingly, sitting itself did not appear to be the main issue, since people who spent long hours seated at mentally engaging jobs often showed healthier brain patterns.

mix_items.title: Scientists found mystery bacteria inside one of the ocean’s most elusive whales
mix_items.summary: Scientists studying decades of pygmy sperm whale strandings have uncovered three previously unknown types of Helicobacter bacteria hiding in the animals’ stomachs. All four infected whales showed serious digestive damage, including inflammation, ulcers, scarring, and parasite infestations, although the bacteria were not confirmed as the cause of death.

mix_items.title: New molecular map reveals how the flu virus hijacks human cells
mix_items.summary: Scientists uncovered how influenza A commandeers human cells, including a surprising strategy that dissolves tiny structures in the nucleus and releases proteins the virus may use to reproduce. The detailed molecular map could reveal new drug targets and help researchers study dangerous flu strains such as H5N1.

mix_items.title: The secret underground system keeping the Grand Canyon alive
mix_items.summary: Scientists are venturing into the Grand Canyon’s hidden cave networks to solve a mystery: how snowmelt travels underground to supply the park’s vital springs. Their discoveries could help protect the canyon’s water from drought, contamination, and other growing threats.

mix_items.title: DNA solves 250-year-old mystery of the Seychelles’ lost crocodiles
mix_items.summary: Scientists have solved the mystery of the Seychelles’ vanished crocodiles using DNA from historic museum specimens. The reptiles were not a unique species after all, but an isolated population of saltwater crocodiles that likely drifted thousands of kilometers across the Indian Ocean.

mix_items.title: Scottish wrens may be evolving into new species through island gigantism
mix_items.summary: Tiny birds on remote Scottish islands are undergoing a dramatic evolutionary transformation. Scientists studying four isolated populations of British Wrens discovered that some island birds have grown astonishingly large — with the biggest St Kilda Wrens weighing more than twice as much as the smallest mainland birds. The research suggests these wrens are evolving independently, developing unique songs, appearances, and genetics that may eventually turn them into entirely new species.

mix_items.title: A New York cemetery was hiding 5.5 million bees underground
mix_items.summary: A casual walk through an Ithaca cemetery led to the discovery of a gigantic hidden bee population — roughly 5.5 million ground-nesting bees packed beneath the soil. Scientists believe it may be one of the largest bee aggregations ever documented and say the insects are crucial pollinators for apple orchards and other crops. The bees have likely lived there for more than 100 years, thriving in the cemetery’s undisturbed sandy soil.

mix_items.title: Earth’s orbital wobble triggered rapid climate chaos during the dinosaur age
mix_items.summary: New research suggests Earth’s climate can swing wildly on surprisingly short timescales — even during hot, ice-free greenhouse periods. By studying ancient sediments from the Late Cretaceous, scientists uncovered repeating climate shifts tied to tiny changes in Earth’s orbital wobble. These cycles may have repeatedly pushed the planet between humid and arid states every few thousand years.
